LLM CALL COST SCAN · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER

Which LLM calls in your code are quietly costing you money?

Paste source code and get every OpenAI, Anthropic and Gemini call that has no output cap, sits inside a loop, hard-codes a premium-tier model where a small sibling often does the job, or uses a retired model name — plus a monthly estimate from your own traffic guess.

Nothing is uploaded. The text box is scanned in this browser and never leaves your device. This reads source text only: it cannot see your real usage or bill.

1. Paste your code

2. What it found

RuleLevelLineDetail

Prefer a CLI, or want this as a CI gate?

Same logic, zero dependencies, one command — walks a whole source tree, skipping node_modules, .git and similar:

node cli.mjs scan src                                   # human-readable
node cli.mjs scan . --json                                 # machine-readable
node cli.mjs scan src --calls-per-day 5000 --out-tokens 500
node cli.mjs scan src --fail-on warn                       # fail CI on warnings too
node cli.mjs scan src --prices my-prices.json              # your negotiated or current prices

Get cli.mjs and engine.mjs — Node 18+, nothing to install, no network call. Exits 1 on a retired model name (or on any warning with --fail-on warn).

What's recognised

VendorCall sites matched

Python and JS/TS, matched line by line. A model passed through a variable is reported as unpriced rather than guessed at. List prices in the built-in table are illustrative and dated; edit them with --prices or the CLI JSON file. More: why LLM bills surprise teams, and what a static scan can and cannot catch.

Common questions

Does this read my API traffic or my bill?

No. It reads source text only, so it can see what your code asks for, not what actually runs. Every dollar figure is arithmetic on a calls-per-day and token guess that you type, multiplied by list prices you can edit. It is an estimate for comparing options, never a measurement of what you are charged.

Why flag a call with no max-tokens?

Without an output cap, one call can generate the model's full output limit. A prompt that accidentally or deliberately asks for a long answer then costs far more than you budgeted, and it does so on every call. A cap is one line and bounds the worst case.

Why flag a premium model if I need it?

It is an information note, not an error. Teams often hard-code the largest model during prototyping and never revisit it. A small-tier sibling from the same vendor frequently handles classification, extraction and short rewrites; run an eval on your own prompts before switching, because quality is yours to verify.

Is my code uploaded anywhere?

No. The browser page scans the text you paste in your own browser and never sends it anywhere. The CLI reads only local files and makes no network call.

Switching models or editing a prompt rather than costing it? Diff saved outputs before and after to catch broken JSON, new refusals and truncation.

We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you type, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record. If a tool needs to survive, get cli.mjs and run it yourself.

Everything runs in your browser. The text you paste is never uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors. Anonymous feature events (scan_run, example_loaded) are counted only in local storage and can be deleted with the button below. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control are honoured.

To enforce a cap at run time rather than in review, LLM Spend Guard refuses a call before it is sent when it would cross a per-user, per-run or daily budget.

Why LLM API bills surprise teams, and what a code scan can catch

An LLM call is billed per token, in and out. Most surprises come from a handful of code shapes that look harmless in review, because the cost is not visible in the diff. Four of them can be found by reading the source.

1. No output cap

Without max_tokens (or max_output_tokens), a single call may generate the model's full output limit. Output tokens are usually priced several times higher than input tokens, so the one unbounded call dominates. A cap is one line and bounds the worst case.

2. A call inside a loop

A call per item is fine for ten items and a surprise for ten thousand. The scan flags calls nested under for, while, .map or forEach so a reviewer asks what bounds the loop, and whether items can share one prompt.

3. A premium model chosen once and never revisited

Prototypes tend to hard-code the largest model. Many production tasks (classification, extraction, short rewrites) are handled by a smaller tier from the same vendor at a fraction of the price. The scan notes the sibling; only an evaluation on your own prompts can say whether it is good enough.

4. A retired model name

Vendors retire model names. A call to a retired name fails at runtime, often in a rarely-exercised code path. The built-in list is short and unambiguous; always confirm on the vendor's deprecations page.

What a static scan cannot see

Cannot seeWhy
Real traffic and prompt lengthOnly your provider's dashboard records them; the estimate here is your own guess times list prices.
Models set through a variable or configReported as unpriced rather than guessed.
Calls hidden behind a wrapper libraryv0 matches the vendors' own SDK call shapes, line by line.
Caching, batching and discount programsList prices only; override with --prices.

Wiring it into CI as a gate

- name: Scan for costly LLM calls
  run: node ventures/llm-call-cost-scan/cli.mjs scan src --fail-on warn

By default only retired model names fail the run. --fail-on warn also fails on uncapped outputs and calls in loops, which is the stricter gate for teams that want every call bounded.

Common questions

Can a static scan tell me what I actually spend?

No. It sees what your code asks for, not how often it runs or how long real prompts are. It can bound the worst case (no output cap) and point at multipliers (a loop), but your provider's usage dashboard is the only record of actual spend.

Is a premium model always wasteful?

No. The scan reports it as a note because prototypes often hard-code the largest model and never revisit it. Whether a smaller tier is good enough is an empirical question about your prompts, so evaluate before switching.

What about SDK wrappers, LangChain or LiteLLM?

v0 matches the vendors' own SDK call shapes. A wrapper that hides the call behind its own function is outside what a line-by-line text scan can see; point the CLI at the wrapper's source or inspect where it sets the model.
